passage:
Mateo was already at his van in the garden-centre car park in Lisbon when he counted the change: thirty euros too much. The cashier must have taken his twenty for a fifty.

Rain was starting. His next delivery was across the river, and nobody at the till would ever know which customer had walked off with it.

He stood there with the notes going damp in his hand, then locked the van and walked back in.

The queue was long. When he reached the front, the name badge said Noa.

"You gave me change for a fifty. I paid with a twenty."

Noa's shoulders dropped. "I'd have been short at closing. Thank you."

He was twelve minutes late to his next drop and got a sharp look for it.

Three weeks later the garden centre needed a regular driver for weekend orders. The manager rang him. "Noa gave us your name. Said you're the honest one."

qa.q: How much extra change did Mateo get?
qa.a: Mateo got thirty euros too much.

qa.q: Why did Mateo stand in the rain with the notes before walking back?
qa.a: He felt tempted and torn: he was running late and nobody would ever know, but keeping money that wasn't his sat badly with him.

qa.q: What small step helped Mateo do the right thing with nobody watching?
qa.a: He locked the van and walked straight back in before he could talk himself out of it; acting quickly kept the choice simple.

qa.q: What was it like for Noa when Mateo returned the money?
qa.a: Noa felt relieved, since the till would have been short at closing, and later trusted Mateo enough to recommend him for the weekend work.

grounding: Shows an adult returning extra change nobody could trace, paying a small cost in time, and later gaining a reputation for being trusted.

subtype: Honouring a colleague who pays the price [Observer]
passage:
You asked why I keep backing Payal in meetings. Here's the story, and yes, it's me, Tarun, the one who stayed quiet at first.

Last quarter our biggest client wanted us to confirm the software had passed its security audit. It hadn't finished. Our manager said, "Just tell them it's done."

Payal said no, calmly. "I can tell them the date it will be done."

The client went elsewhere. In March the team-lead post went to someone else, and everyone knew why.

For a week she ate lunch alone at her desk. I kept thinking she must feel like the only fool in the building, and that the rest of us had let her be one.

So I took my lunch to her desk. In the review meeting I said out loud that she had kept us from a false claim. Two others backed me.

It didn't get her the post. But she told me the lunches mattered more than she expected, and it has changed how I'll answer the next time someone asks me to fudge something.

qa.q: What did Payal offer to tell the client instead?
qa.a: Payal said she could tell them the date it will be done.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel while watching Payal eat lunch alone?
qa.a: Tarun felt uneasy and guilty, imagining she must feel like the only fool in the building and that the others, Tarun included, had let her be one.

qa.q: How could colleagues support someone who pays a price for honesty?
qa.a: Sit with them, say publicly what their honesty protected the team from, and back them in meetings, so they are not left standing alone.

qa.q: What was it like for Payal when colleagues backed her in the review meeting?
qa.a: Payal felt less isolated; she later said the lunches mattered more than she expected, even though the post still went to someone else.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague who watches a teammate lose a client and a promotion for refusing to lie, and supports her openly so honesty is not a lonely choice.

passage:
I'm Madhav, and I still think about that phone call.

Gargi had been sleeping on my sofa for four days. She had left her ex after months of him checking her phone and turning up at her office. On the fifth evening he rang me. "Is she with you? Just tell me where she is."

The easy answer was "No idea." A clean lie, and it would protect her.

But I thought about who it touched: Gargi first; me, if he found out and came to my door; and my own habit of saying whatever works in the moment.

So I said, "I'm not going to tell you anything about Gargi. Please stop calling me." I hung up and blocked the number.

My hands were shaking. That same night Gargi and I rang a women's helpline together, and the next morning she went to the police station with her sister.

It was my choice not to answer him. If he is angry, that is mine to carry. I would choose it again.

qa.q: On which evening did Gargi's ex ring Madhav?
qa.a: He rang on the fifth evening, after Gargi had been sleeping on the sofa for four days.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling after hanging up?
qa.a: Madhav was shaken, hands shaking, yet settled about the choice, enough to say they would choose it again.
Refusing to share anything instead of lying, then blocking the number and ringing a helpline that same night; it kept Gargi safe without a lie Madhav would have to keep up.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel knowing Madhav told her ex nothing?
qa.a: Gargi would likely feel safer and supported, since her whereabouts stayed protected and she was not alone when she rang the helpline.

grounding: Shows a person weighing honesty against protecting someone from harm, choosing an open refusal over a lie, involving a helpline, and owning the choice.
